transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Linda Kenyon.
For the second straight day, Houthi rebels have attacked the airport in Saudi Arabia's capital.
NPR's Aya Batrawi reports one person was killed, 11 others injured.
Saudi authorities say the deadliest attack in years took place Saturday when a passenger terminal in the capital Riyadh was hit,
killing at least 13 people and wounding more than 300 others.
The attacks have suspended operations at Riyadh airport
and forced oil executives from major companies to cancel their attendance at an energy summit in the capital this week.
The Houthis say they're attacking Saudi airports and Aramco energy sites with missiles and drones
in response to Saudi airstrikes on Yemen that have killed civilians there too.
The Houthis, who are backed by Iran, are also blocking Saudi oil tankers from using the Red Sea shipping strait.
The foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia and Iran held a call on Sunday to discuss the recent escalation.
Aya Batrawi, NPR News, Dubai.
President Trump says he secured an energy ceasefire deal with Russia that would pause airstrikes against energy sites.
Ukraine's President Zelensky says Ukraine will stop the attacks if Russia does the same.
If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system
and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people.
Speaking at the Warsaw security forum in Poland, President Zelensky said following Trump's statement about the ceasefire,
Russia struck Ukrainian energy facilities again, including a power plant in Kharkiv and a civilian gas station.
He also said he did not hear from President Trump about the ceasefire; he learned about it on social media.
Three of South Carolina's candidates for U.S. Senate made their cases to voters last night.
South Carolina Public Radio's Luis Alfredo Garcia reports this was their only confirmed debate before the November midterms.
Republican Senator Darlene Graham and Democratic pediatrician Dr. Annie Andrews spent a good chunk of their given debate time talking about each other.
Libertarian Casey Whitener mostly stuck to answering moderator questions.
But the two leading candidates did give direct, different answers on how the United States should navigate its policy with Israel.
Graham says the country needs to stand with its "strongest ally" in the Middle East, and she condemned Hamas.
Andrews highlighted humanitarian concerns in the region.
Israelis deserve a safe place to live, and Palestinians also deserve to live in peace.
What's happening in the region is devastating. It is a humanitarian crisis.
The winner of the race will be the first woman elected to represent South Carolina in the Senate.
For NPR News, I'm Luis Alfredo Garcia in Columbia, South Carolina.
Darlene Graham is the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
You're listening to NPR News.
The U.S. is in the midst of the biggest and deadliest measles epidemic in decades.
With cases reported across the country, infectious disease experts say some vaccinated adults should consider getting another measles vaccine.
NPR's Maria Godoy has more.
Before vaccines, measles used to kill four to five hundred people in the U.S. each year.
Two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine is ninety-seven percent effective.
Most people vaccinated before 1989 probably received just one dose instead of the two doses recommended for children today.
Dr. Larry Kociolek of Northwestern University says traditionally,
one dose has been considered sufficient protection for adults not at high risk, but he says these days...
If you are living in areas with high measles activity, it does make a whole lot of sense for adults to go ahead and get that second dose.
If you're not sure of your vaccination history, he says there's no harm in getting an extra dose of the MMR vaccine.
Maria Godoy, NPR News.
China's passenger car exports are booming, rising sixty-four percent in September, compared with the same period last year.
China exported nearly nine hundred twenty thousand passenger vehicles last month,
helped by strong demand for plug-in hybrids and electric vehicles.
Exports in the first nine months of the year exceeded seven point one million vehicles.
Weaker consumer confidence and reduced government subsidies had weighed in on domestic sales,
prompting China automakers to target markets elsewhere.
I'm Lyndi Kenyon, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Houthi rebels attack Riyadh airport for second day, killing at least 13 people
President Trump announces energy ceasefire deal with Russia; Zelensky says Ukraine will reciprocate
Three South Carolina Senate candidates debate, including Darlene Graham and Annie Andrews, on Israel policy
U.S. measles epidemic prompts experts to urge some vaccinated adults to get second MMR dose
China's passenger car exports rise 64% in September, driven by plug-in hybrids and EVs
